title: MSCE Biology: examinable topics and how they are weighted
subtitle: A study outline drawn from the national syllabus — use it to check coverage, not to replace the syllabus

blocks.text: This is a checklist of the topics that carry marks in MSCE Biology, with a note on where each one usually appears. Tick a topic only when you can answer a past-paper question on it without notes. A topic you recognise but cannot write about is not yet covered.
The official syllabus remains the authority on content and assessment. This outline is a revision map written for Kuphanda, and it does not reproduce the syllabus document.
Topics, what to be able to do, and where it appears
rows: Label plant and animal cells; state the function of each organelle
Movement in and out of cells
Explain diffusion, osmosis and active transport with examples
Describe effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity
Write the equation; describe the effect of light, CO2 and temperature
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in yeast and muscle

items: Define gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, dominant and recessive.
Complete a monohybrid cross, including a Punnett square, and state the ratio.
Describe the structure of DNA and the base-pairing rule.
Explain the difference between continuous and discontinuous variation, with examples.
Describe causes of mutation and give one named example with its effect.

rows: Construct and interpret; explain energy loss between levels
Describe the carbon and nitrogen cycles
Explain causes and effects of deforestation and soil erosion

blocks.text: Human systems are the largest single block of Paper 2. Expect one structured question on transport or gaseous exchange, and one on reproduction or the kidney. Learn the diagram, then learn the sequence: what enters, what is exchanged, what leaves.

items: Digestion: enzymes at each stage, and where each is produced.
Transport: heart structure, double circulation, blood components.
Gaseous exchange: alveoli structure and the effect of smoking.
Excretion: nephron structure and the effect of ADH.
Reproduction: menstrual cycle, fertilisation, placenta and birth.

rows: Two Paper 1 sections at 80% or better
A full monohybrid question marked against a scheme
One structured question per topic, timed
Two full papers under exam conditions
A short test on each topic you got wrong

blocks.text: Mark your own work against a scheme before you look at the answers. The gap between what you wrote and what the scheme rewards is the most useful information you will get all week.
